title: The Enduring Persistence of Neuromyths in Education
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick uses a new survey of more than 3,000 Spanish teachers by Fernández and colleagues to argue that the profession is still caught between intuition and evidence. Starting from the Dekker finding that nine in ten teachers believed in learning styles, he notes that the new study goes beyond brain myths to misconceptions about everyday teaching methods. He qualifies some of its classifications, separating general-transfer claims for motor-perception drills from real embodied-cognition findings, and defending discovery approaches in the early years. His main move is to read the study's factor analysis as evidence that misconceptions form coherent mental models, so that correcting one myth in isolation may achieve little. He also identifies a 'metacognitive blindness' in teachers who underrate how poorly students judge their own knowledge. He ends on equity, arguing that discovery learning and similar ideas cost disadvantaged pupils most and that good intentions are not a substitute for evidence.
points: Hendrick compares teachers' endorsement of learning styles with doctors still believing in miasma, to show how little alarm debunked ideas cause in education.

The most-endorsed misconception, that motor-perception exercises improve general cognition, is analysed as a false promise of general transfer, which he distinguishes from legitimate links between movement and learning.
The factor analysis showing myths clustering across topics leads him to argue that misconceptions are part of teachers' professional identity and resemble political or religious conviction.
Teachers' failure to accept that students are poor judges of their own knowledge is traced to classroom emotional dynamics and to teachers sharing the same metacognitive illusions.
He argues that discovery learning may suit preschool but becomes 'educational malpractice' for disadvantaged older students who lack the background knowledge to discover what others absorbed at home.
quotes: Imagine, for a moment, that nine out of ten doctors still believed that illness was caused by miasma (bad air) rather than bacteria or viruses. We would be appalled; we would question whether medicine as a profession had any meaningful relationship with evidence at all. Yet in education, such widespread endorsement of debunked ideas barely raises an eyebrow.

What’s striking in this study is that when researchers broadened the scope beyond the brain, they found just as many unsupported ideas about basic teaching methods and dayItoIday classroom decisions. These aren’t fringe ideas; they are widespread beliefs shaping classroom practice today.

The real issue is the promise of general transfer, the idea that practising specific motor skills will improve unrelated cognitive abilities. What teachers may be missing is the distinction between movement that supports learning in context versus decontextualised exercises that claim to boost overall brainpower.

The authors’ analysis suggests that misconceptions are not isolated errors but components of larger mental models: coherent, but often scientifically inaccurate, worldviews about learning. And here’s the worrying implication: Correcting a single myth in isolation may have little impact if the underlying belief system remains intact.
Another reason may be that teachers themselves share the same metacognitive illusions. Research shows that even experienced professionals overestimate their ability to gauge understanding in others.

Discovery learning might work for middle-class children who arrive at school with extensive vocabulary and background knowledge. But for disadvantaged students, it can be a form of educational malpractice, expecting them to reinvent what others learned through cultural osmosis, perpetuating rather than reducing educational inequality.

This doesn't mean abandoning our values or treating children as empty vessels. But it does mean recognising that good intentions are not enough, that feeling right is not the same as being right, and that the most caring thing we can do for students is to use approaches that actually help them learn.
